summary: An update to the Network Working Group's documentation conventions, revising earlier notes (RFC 10 and RFC 16) about how the group's notes are written and distributed. Later revisions followed in RFC 27 and RFC 30.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains how the Network Working Group can write and circulate informal notes. It encourages useful ideas to be shared promptly, even when they are not polished or authoritative.

questions: what were the nwg documentation conventions
what information should an rfc note include
subtitle: Sets practical conventions for writing and distributing Network Working Group notes.

tldr.problem: The Network Working Group needed conventions for publishing notes without making every note seem authoritative or requiring polished prose.
tldr.mechanism: The memo allows broad subject matter and informal, timely writing, while asking each note to include a serial number, author and affiliation, date, and title.
tldr.outcome: The note defines lightweight expectations for content, format, and distribution. Unit metadata lists RFCs 27 and 30 as updates.

today: RFC 24 is an early documentation-conventions note, and the unit metadata lists RFCs 27 and 30 as updates to it.

sections.title: What an NWG Note Can Contain
sections.content:
A Network Working Group note may discuss any idea related to host software, network use, or another network topic. Notes should be timely rather than polished, and they may include questions, suggestions, or implementation details without a complete formal argument.

The memo says a note can be as short as one sentence. It explains that flexible rules can reduce the tendency to treat every written statement as authoritative and can make authors less hesitant to publish unfinished ideas.
sections.plainLanguage: An NWG note can share an idea before it is fully polished. This helps people discuss network questions without treating every note as a final decision.

sections.title: Basic Format and Distribution
sections.content:
Each note should identify the Network Working Group, its RFC serial number, the author and affiliation, the date, and a title. Titles do not have to be unique, and Steve Crocker at UCLA assigns serial numbers.

The author sends one copy from their site to the listed NWG members. Local reproduction can provide any additional copies that are needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A note needs a few details so readers can identify who wrote it and when. The author sends one copy to each person on the distribution list, and recipients can make local copies.

sections.title: An Open Working Group
sections.content:
The Network Working Group consists of interested people from existing or potential ARPA Network sites, and membership is not closed. Its work includes host software, network-use strategies, and experience with the network.

The memo frames its conventions as a way to encourage discussion, not as a claim that every note is official or complete.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone interested from a current or potential network site can take part. The notes are meant to support discussion and shared learning.
